analysis.title: Global Equities: A US Rotation Story Becomes A Correlation Story
key_insights: The sell-off began in semiconductors and has spread to the wider market. The S&P 500 fell 4.36% to 7,353 on Nov 5, with 376 decliners vs 127 advancers. The desk says the key signal is rising correlation underneath the moves, plus a technical breakdown, not just their size.

The move is predominantly US. The S&P 500 is down 4.0% over two weeks while the HSCEI is up 8.8%, Hang Seng +8.2%, CSI 300 +2.0% and Euro Stoxx 50 +2.5%. The desk frames it as a repricing of the US multiple premium and US geographic positioning against a changed political and geopolitical backdrop after the midterms.

The desk says to park fundamentals and focus on positioning. Memory fell 16% in a day but is still up 78% this year. Ownership, crowding, liquidity and who is forced to sell matter more than the next turn of the earnings multiple.

No capitulation is visible in the US complex. Volume is below July levels (Nvidia 9% below, Micron 38% below, Samsung 50% below), which the desk reads as persistent distribution rather than forced liquidation. Intel is the exception, with volume 45% above July.

The buyers who ended the July deleveraging (CTAs, retail and especially long-only accounts that missed the first AI leg) are not visible yet. Hedge fund activity on the desk is much higher than long-only, and most long-only axes are tickets from earlier in the week. Leverage is cleaner than in July, but that does not by itself create a buyer.

Correlation is the pain trade. Inverse relationships such as semis vs software and semis vs hyperscalers are called near irrational territory. Apparent hedges (software, hyperscalers, defensives, AAPL as an anti-AI trade) could become funding sources as gross exposure comes down, since you can only sell what you own.

The equity/bond hedge has weakened: the S&P 500/10-year correlation moved from -0.34 in July to +0.23. Brent is near $100 and acts as a macro headwind. Easing oil or geopolitical risk would favor Europe, Asia, cyclicals and consumer. Higher oil would intensify cross-asset pressure.

Semis are falling at COVID speed. The SOX is well below its 200-day average and is down 31.8% peak-to-trough in 22 trading days. The Nasdaq 100 is down 14.7% over the same period, more than its whole 10.9% July drawdown in about half the time. US semis (Intel, AMD, Nvidia) have fallen further than in July, while ASML, Infineon and STMicro remain inside their July lows.

Breadth of damage: the median S&P 500 stock is still up 0.94% over two weeks, but 26 constituents are down more than 20% and 72 more than 10%. Caterpillar is the most oversold S&P stock (RSI 19.5). ServiceNow is down 35%, Datadog 32%, Marvell 40% and Intel 39%.

Desk positioning view: nibble at semis vs defensive tech, and sell the recent hedging beneficiaries against it. Lean against extreme relative moves (semis vs software, US vs European semis, defensives vs cyclicals, geographic spreads) rather than call an index low, especially in the US. Squeezes are possible, but negative headlines, especially tech headlines, will carry more weight and last longer.

Client feedback: the initial post-midterm read was a clearing event rather than a regime change. Clients hold cash but are slow to deploy it, hedge funds are more willing to add risk, and long-only managers are on the sidelines. Behavior is rotation, not re-grossing. Clients cite oil and the geopolitical risk premium as bigger catalysts than US political headlines. Views on AI data-centre exposure are split. Themes of interest are defence and aerospace, European banks and Asian tech, with skepticism on the renewables rally.
Credit stress is emerging but modest: iTraxx at 62bps, +12bps. The desk notes that, unlike dot-com and COVID, there is no policy easing (no cut, yields rising) and the bond hedge is broken.

sector_views.rationale: The desk would start nibbling at semis vs defensive tech after a COVID-speed drop, but sees no capitulation or long-only buyers yet.
Crowded hedges that could become funding sources as correlations rise.
They benefit from lower oil and from a rotation away from the US multiple premium. Clients cite European banks, defence and aerospace, and Asian tech as interesting.

macro_indicators.interpretation: The bond hedge for equities has stopped working because bonds are falling with equities.
A direct macro headwind, not a shock absorber. Oil is a key cross-asset variable.
Credit stress is emerging but moderate.

trade_ideas.description: Buy some semiconductors (nibble) vs defensive tech, and sell the recent hedging beneficiaries against it
trade_ideas.rationale: Inverse correlations of semis vs software and hyperscalers are near irrational territory, and some hedges could become funding sources.
trade_ideas.risk: No capitulation or long-only buyers yet. Negative tech headlines may weigh longer.

trade_ideas.description: Lean against extreme relative moves: semis vs software, US vs European semis, defensives vs cyclicals, geographic spreads
trade_ideas.rationale: Opportunity is in dislocation and positioning rather than calling an index low.
trade_ideas.risk: Not a call on an index bottom, especially in the US.

risk_factors: Rising correlation turns the sell-off into broad portfolio risk and weakens rotational hedges.
No long-only buyers to absorb selling as in July.
Oil moving higher again would intensify cross-asset pressure.
Bonds falling with equities with no policy easing (no cut, yields rising).
Negative tech headlines carry asymmetric weight in a fragile market.
vol_and_positioning: The VIX closed at 28.2 on Nov 5, up from 14.8 on Oct 9, and is described as comparable to the level just before the COVID volatility spike.
Leverage is materially cleaner than in July, but long-only demand is absent. Volume is below July levels in most key names.

Defensives are crowded, bonds are falling with equities and rotational hedges risk becoming funding sources. Watch list: VIX, Nvidia/Micron/ASML volume vs July, SOX vs its 200-day average, Brent, S&P/10-year correlation, and whether long-only accounts start buying.
geopolitical: The desk cites this week's political developments after the US midterms as a potentially significant change in the political and geopolitical landscape, bearing on the risk premium for the US versus the rest of the world.
The desk refers to a 'Trump put' as more of a tailwind for rest-of-world markets through potentially lower oil than for broader tech.
Geopolitical risk premium in oil is cited by clients as a more important catalyst than US political headlines.

tension_points.bull_case: Semis are down at COVID speed, the SOX is well below its 200-day average, inverse correlations versus software and hyperscalers are near irrational, and leverage is cleaner than in July. The desk would nibble at semis vs defensive tech.
tension_points.bear_case: No capitulation: volume is below July levels in Nvidia, Micron and Samsung, and no long-only buyers have appeared. Correlation is rising and hedges may become funding sources.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Nvidia, Micron or ASML volume reaching or exceeding July levels would signal a flush, and long-only accounts starting to buy would signal demand. Further oil strength, or Brent moving higher again, would intensify pressure.

theme_stances.key_argument: The market is moving from a rotation story to a correlation story, and hedges that worked may become funding sources.
theme_stances.evidence: The biggest pain trade from here may simply be correlation itself.

theme_stances.key_argument: Investors are reconsidering the premium paid for US exposure after the political shift, and lower oil helps the rest of the world.
theme_stances.evidence: a substantial rotation away from extreme US geographic positioning and the US multiple premium

theme_stances.key_argument: July's sell-off ended when long-only accounts bought; that demand is not visible yet.
theme_stances.evidence: The key thing I am watching now is who steps in to buy.
